passages.t: ‘By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept’
passages.happening:
Psalm 137 has no heading. It begins with a memory. “By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (verse 1). “There on the willows we hung our harps” (verse 2).

Their captors wanted entertainment. They hung up their harps, they say, “for there our captors requested a song; our tormentors demanded songs of joy: ‘Sing us a song of Zion’” (verse 3).

The singers could not do it. “How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Its first line tells us roughly when it was written. It comes after the army of Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC and took many of its people away, as the book page says in its part on dates. The exiles were settled in southern Mesopotamia, a land of rivers and canals. The prophet Ezekiel was “among the exiles by the River Kebar” (Ezekiel 1:1). The past tense, ‘we sat and wept’, makes many readers think the psalm was written after the exile, by someone looking back. Others think it was written in Babylon.

What had they lost? Not only homes. The Babylonians “burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 25:9). The king's sons were killed in front of him (2 Kings 25:7). Lamentations remembers “children and infants” fainting “in the streets of the city” (Lamentations 2:11).

The harp was the instrument of temple music, and of David. Hanging it up was a refusal to play. The ‘songs of Zion’ were hymns about God's city, some of which sang that God would never let it fall (Psalms 46 and 48). To sing them for laughs, in the capital of the empire that had just burned Zion, was more than they could bear.
passages.later:
God told the same exiles, through Jeremiah, to settle down and pray for the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7). Their grief and their prayers for their captors stand side by side in the Bible.

Christians have taken the exiles' longing as a picture of their own. Hebrews says that the faithful “were longing for a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and that “here we do not have a permanent city” (Hebrews 13:14).
passages.asks:
Psalm 137 honours grief. It does not hurry the exiles to cheer up, and it does not shame them for being unable to sing. Some losses are too deep for songs of joy, and pretending otherwise would be a lie.

Have you been asked to smile while you were grieving? This psalm gives you words for that. You are allowed to hang up your harp for a while. God hears the silence too.

passages.happening: Now the singer makes a vow. “If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function” (verse 5). “May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember you, if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy!” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This is a self-curse, a common way of making a solemn promise in the ancient world: may this happen to me if I break my word. Notice what the singer puts at stake. A harpist plays with his right hand and sings with his tongue. He is saying: let me lose my music, my craft, my voice, if I ever forget.

So the refusal in verse 4 was not forgetfulness. The exiles would not sing Zion's songs for their captors, but they would never stop remembering Zion. They would keep the songs for the LORD.

Jerusalem here is more than a place on a map. It was the city where God had chosen to put his name, the place of the temple and of worship. To forget it would be to forget God's promises.

This psalm has a long life in Jewish prayer. In many Jewish homes it has been the custom to say Psalm 137 before the blessing after meals on ordinary weekdays, in memory of the temple's fall, and to say Psalm 126, the song of return, on Sabbaths and feast days. The weekday custom is less common now.
passages.later: Paul wrote that believers' “citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). John saw a new Jerusalem coming down from God (Revelation 21:2). Christians who pray verses 5 and 6 may pray them of God's city and God's people.
passages.asks:
What do you refuse to forget? Psalm 137 shows people who held on to God's promises when everything they could see said those promises were finished.

Memory can be an act of faith. When you remember what God has said and done, even far from home, you are saying that his word still stands.

passages.t: ‘Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom’, and the hardest lines in the Psalms
passages.happening:
The psalm ends with two cries for justice. First, against Edom, Israel's neighbour. “Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell: ‘Destroy it,’ they said, ‘tear it down to its foundations!’” (verse 7).

Then against Babylon itself. “O Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us” (verse 8). And the last line: “Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Edom was descended from Esau, Jacob's brother. When Jerusalem fell, the Edomites cheered the enemy on. The prophet Obadiah says to Edom, “On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth” (Obadiah 1:11), you were like one of them.

‘Daughter of Babylon’ means the city and its people. ‘As you have done to us’ is the key to verse 9. These are the words of people who had seen their own children killed. The king's sons were slaughtered before his eyes (2 Kings 25:7). In the siege, children died in the streets (Lamentations 2:11). The people singing this psalm are asking God to repay Babylon in kind.

They were not the first to say it. Isaiah had already spoken of Babylon's fall in the same terrible words: “Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes” (Isaiah 13:16). Jeremiah heard God say, “I will repay Babylon” (Jeremiah 51:24). Ancient war was brutal, and conquering armies did kill children. The psalm uses the language of the war that had been done to them.

No modern nation is in view in these verses, and they say nothing against the people of any land today.
passages.later:
In Revelation, ‘Babylon’ becomes the name for every proud power that crushes God's people: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (Revelation 18:2). And the martyrs cry, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10).

Paul tells believers, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19). And Jesus prayed for those who killed him, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).
passages.hard:
Verse 9 is listed on the book page among the hardest lines in the Bible. It should not be softened, and it should not be explained away. It calls ‘blessed’ whoever kills the children of Babylon. No one should read it without a shudder.

What it is: the cry of people who had seen their own children killed (2 Kings 25:7; Lamentations 2:11), asking God to repay Babylon in kind, in words a prophet had already used against Babylon (Isaiah 13:16). It is a prayer spoken to God. It is not a command to anyone.

The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out four ways Christians read lines like this, and these notes do not choose between them. Some read it as honest prayer that hands vengeance to God instead of taking it. Some read it as the voice of the oppressed, which those who have never suffered so should be slow to judge. Some, like Dietrich Bonhoeffer, read such prayers in the light of the cross, where God's judgment and his forgiveness meet. Some, like C. S. Lewis, say plainly that the spirit of such lines is wrong, and that Scripture records them honestly without asking us to pray them. Jewish readers have wrestled with this verse too, and modern Jewish writers have debated it openly.

One thing is not open. No reading of these psalms has ever made it right to harm anyone, least of all a child.

If you carry rage at what was done to you, or to someone you love, this psalm shows that God can hear even that. Your rage is heard. Hand it to God rather than to your own hands. Tell a trusted person: a pastor, a friend, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or fear you might hurt someone, get help today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Psalm 137 does not let us pretend that people of faith never feel hatred. They do, especially when they have been terribly wronged. The psalm takes that hatred to God, out loud, instead of acting on it.

What do you do with your anger? Paul says, “Be angry, yet do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). The psalm and the cross together show the way: tell God the truth about what was done, leave the judging to him, and ask him for what only he can give.
